title: What Does Flow-Matching Bring to TD-Learning?
claim: Iterative integration of a learned field dampens early errors and absorbs shifting targets, preserving earlier features and improving plasticity.
layout: 2 panels, left-to-right, trajectory plot beside layered network diagram with legend
description: Two-panel cartoon. The left panel is a schematic plot with time t on the horizontal axis, between a noise boundary and a Q-value boundary. Blue wavy integration trajectories run inside a shaded grey cone toward a TD target. Yellow dots mark points on a trajectory, with black arrows for the velocity field v_θ(z). Orange ticks mark the interval bounds l and u. A big red upward arrow reads 'Target changes'. The caption beneath reads 'Errors in integration cancel (test-time recovery)'. The right panel shows the training progression Q_θ → Q_θ' → … above a stacked three-block network. The blocks run from a thick-outlined dark yellow block at the bottom to a pale cream block at the top. Inputs (s,a) and z_t feed in at the bottom and z_{t+1} comes out at the top. A dashed loop labelled 'Integration process' feeds the output back to the input. A legend contrasts slow-change blocks with fast-change blocks. The caption beneath reads 'plasticity'. The eye goes first to the red arrow and the trajectories.
caption: Flow-matching critics with non-stationary TD targets. Values are computed by integrating a learned velocity field over multiple steps. This iterative process enables test-time recovery (left), where errors in early integration steps are dampened by later steps. When TD targets change (𝜃→𝜃′), the integration dynamics can absorb part of the shift, allowing earlier features to remain largely unchanged, improving plasticity.
abstract: Recent work shows that flow matching can be effective for scalar Q-value function estimation in reinforcement learning (RL), but it remains unclear why or how this approach differs from standard critics. Contrary to conventional belief, we show that their success is not explained by distributional RL, as explicitly modeling return distributions can reduce performance. Instead, we argue that the use of integration for reading out values and dense velocity supervision at each step of this integration process for training improves TD learning via two mechanisms. First, it enables robust value prediction through \emph{test-time recovery}, whereby iterative computation through integration dampens errors in early value estimates as more integration steps are performed. This recovery mechanism is absent in monolithic critics. Second, supervising the velocity field at multiple interpolant values induces more \emph{plastic} feature learning within the network, allowing critics to represent non-stationary TD targets without discarding previously learned features or overfitting to individual TD targets encountered during training. We formalize these effects and validate them empirically, showing that flow-matching critics substantially outperform monolithic critics (2$\times$ in final performance and around 5$\times$ in sample efficiency) in settings where loss of plasticity poses a challenge e.g., in high-UTD online RL problems, while remaining stable during learning.
